newsitem.title: INDIA: Rice - India, Vietnam gear up for export sales.
newsitem.headline: Rice - India, Vietnam gear up for export sales.

text.p: Robust demand has boosted the rice trade in India and Vietnam with a slew of contracts and shipments headed for Africa, Latin America and the Middle East, traders said on Thursday.
Indian rice exporters have started signing forward contracts in anticipation of a bumper rice harvest beginning in early October, the traders said.
"A good harvest is expected and contracts are signed to export from the new crop," said Prem Garg, a leading foodgrains exporter in New Delhi.
Indian traders said the contracts for October shipments started at around US$15-$30 a tonne less than current shipments.
Indian five percent long grain non-Basmati rice for October shipment was quoted at $285-$290 a tonne FOB, 10 percent at $275, 15 percent at $250 and 25 percent at $235, they said.
"The export demand is mainly for the five percent and 10 percent broken varieties. In the lower grades our prices are much higher than Vietnam prices," Garg said.
"Our only hope is to export higher grades like five percent, 10 percent, 15 percent," said Mulraj Tanna, a leading exporter from Bombay. "In lower varieties, we are outpriced."
Traders said Vietnamese exporters were benefitting from relatively low prices and from the Indian crop not yet coming into the market.
Vietnam's official media said this week rice exports in the first nine months of 1996 were estimated at 2.15 million tonnes. For the whole of 1995, exports were 2.025 million tonnes.
They said that since the start of September, the Philippines, Sri Lanka and Senegal had between them ordered more than 50,000 tonnes of low quality rice from Vietnam.
Traders said they expected shipments to total around 300,000 tonnes this month.
The Ministry of Agriculture has asked for the export quota this year to be increased to 2.3-2.5 million tonnes from two million in 1995.
"It's not really a big problem," said one trader. "If exporters want to sell more, they'll get the quota."
Recent flooding in northern and central Vietnam submerged hundreds of thousands of paddy fields, but damage to crops was light because harvesting was almost over when the flooding hit.
"Prices for all grades are starting to firm up," said one trader. "Sales have really been pretty strong this month."
Five-percent broken grade was quoted at $280-$283 a tonne and 10-percent at $265-$270, both little changed from last week.
The situation was not as rosy in Thailand, where the market remained quiet as exporters slowed down buying and awaited an easing of prices, trade sources said.
While benchmark 100 percent white B rice prices dipped slightly, prices of premium grade fragrant rice rose sharply.
The benchmark 100 percent white B was quoted at around US$335-$340 per tonne FOB Bangkok compared with $338-$340 last week.

Fragrant rice was quoted at around $600 a tonne FOB Bangkok compared with $585 last week and an average of $528 in August as supplies were tight amid depleting stocks due to brisk demand in recent months.
Traders said exporters slowed down buying of 100 percent white B grade in a bid to force prices down. Demand also eased as foreign buyers were sidelined by high prices.
But the prices barely dropped because only small supplies entered the market as millers slowed down activity to support the market.
"The prices of Thai rice are too high compared with those of Vietnam and India. It doesn't give much incentive to buy at the moment," said one trader.
